vignette:
She is a 57-year-old Latin American woman who has spent most of her adult life in detective work, a field that has taught her to stay alert, read a room quickly, and trust her instincts before she trusts other people. She comes to the story of her trauma with the same steady, factual voice she uses when she describes an investigation, though as she speaks, it becomes clear that the event has split her life into before and after.

The exposure happens while she is on duty, following a lead in a warehouse where illegal chemicals are being stored. She remembers the sharp, strange smell first, then the way her throat tightens and her eyes start to burn. At the time, she assumes it is only irritation, something she can push through the way she has pushed through exhaustion and danger before. But within minutes she is coughing so hard she cannot get a full breath, and her skin feels hot and prickling, as if she has been pressed against something caustic. Her partner gets her out, and she is taken for emergency treatment, but even as the physical crisis passes, she feels shaken in a way she does not know how to name. She is used to crime scenes, violence, and tension, yet this is different; her own body has become the scene of the threat.

In the days after, she tries to return to her usual pace, but the body she once relied on begins to feel unpredictable. Ordinary smells-cleaning products, fuel, bleach, even some perfumes-can make her chest tighten. She notices that she scans every enclosed space before entering, checking for exits, vents, and anything that might hold fumes. At work, she keeps her mask nearby and becomes irritated when colleagues joke about her caution. She does not tell them how quickly her mind goes back to the warehouse: the grit in her mouth, the panic of not being able to breathe, the helplessness of waiting for help. She has always prided herself on control, on being the one who stays clear-headed when others panic, and she feels ashamed that this memory can still pull her under so easily.

Her sleep changes. She falls asleep exhausted, then wakes abruptly with her heart pounding, sometimes from dreams she cannot fully remember and sometimes from a vague sense that something is in the room with her. When she does sleep, she often dreams of being trapped behind a sealed door or moving through a corridor that fills with invisible gas. In the morning, she feels unrefreshed and tense, as if she has been working through the night instead of resting. She becomes more jumpy at work, reacting sharply when someone approaches from behind or when a colleague opens a cabinet and the sharp scent of disinfectant fills the air. She says she knows she is overreacting, but her body does not seem interested in reassurance.

Over time, she begins to avoid situations that remind her of the exposure, though she frames it as being practical. She asks others to handle certain evidence rooms, hesitates before entering basements or older buildings, and limits time around industrial sites whenever she can. Outside of work, she catches herself choosing routes that keep her away from chemical plants and hardware stores. She becomes more isolated, turning down invitations from friends and from the small circle of family members who ask why she seems "so serious lately." After her divorce, she had already grown used to carrying a great deal alone, but now that independence feels less like strength and more like a narrowing of her world.

What troubles her most is the way the event has altered her sense of safety in her own body. She says that before the exposure, pain or danger always seemed to come from outside and could be managed with training and composure. Now she is not sure when her breathing will suddenly catch, or whether a smell in an ordinary place will send her back into that warehouse. She continues to work, to dress professionally, to speak with authority, but there is a guardedness in her movements and a constant vigilance in her eyes. Even on calmer days, she seems to be listening for something just out of sight, as if part of her is still standing in that contaminated air, waiting for the moment it reaches her again.
